newsitem.title: USA: Cuban dissident faults U.S. policy.
newsitem.headline: Cuban dissident faults U.S. policy.

text.p: A leading Cuban dissident urged Washington to normalise ties with Havana, saying the political transformation of Cuba was inevitable but it must involve President Fidel Castro.

U.S. policy against Castro's communist government had failed and needed to take a new course, Elizardo Sanchez Santa Cruz, head of the Cuban Commission for Human Rights and National Reconciliation in Havana, said on Wednesday night.
"Both governments must be very creative to move out of the morass which relations are in at this point," he said.

Sanchez was speaking at the University of Miami's North-South Centre after a tour of Europe in which he was awarded a prestigious human rights award by French President Jacques Chirac and met several other government leaders.

He is one of the most prominent figures in Cuba's internal opposition. But his views run counter to Washington's current policy, which attempts to isolate Cuba and force Castro's overthrow, and to many in Miami's Cuban exile groups, who view the 70-year-old revolutionary leader as evil incarnate.
Washington last month unveiled a plan pledging billions of dollars in bilateral aid to Cuba -- after Castro is gone.
Sanchez said although Cuba badly needed aid, the plan was flawed. Political change that sought to exclude Castro and the present government was not only impossible but dangerous.

"I have no doubt that transition in Cuba is inevitable but it must be peaceful ... it cannot happen with guns. It must be at the negotiating table. We must work with the present personalities and government. If we say people must be excluded that will be the end of it," he said.
Several Cuban Americans in the audience accused Sanchez of "daydreaming" -- a view many Cuba analysts hold of the exiles' hopes for Castro's downfall.
"The sector I represent within the Cuban dissident movement favours the type of transition that will cost the fewest lives possible," he said.

Sanchez has spent more than eight years in Cuban jails for his political and human rights work. He was dismissed as a history and philosophy professor at Havana University in 1968 and founded the human rights commission in 1987.

He said the commission faced constant harassment from the authorities -- "It is a daily war." The human right situation had worsened over the past year, he said, pointing to a recent crackdown against independent journalists.

Castro still enjoys popular support, although he might lose an election if one was ever held, he said. Most Cubans now wanted change of some sort, including nearly all the intellectuals and many government officials.
